rationale: A wins because it keeps the causal trap visible: "invites a reporter to test whether one is paying for the other" is the right posture. B's strongest headline, "Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices," turns an inference into a premise, then props it up with "the prevailing belief right now" that the update does not establish. A still overreaches on the Digital Makeline, but its proof lists and uncomfortable questions would keep a founder from face-planting on a reporter call.
gaps_in_A: "first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format" is overclaimed. The update gives one prep robot rolling to 100 stores and one bowl system still in testing, not proof of a full-line automation architecture.
"Other operators watching this decide their own capex from it" assumes market reaction the update does not provide.

"The investor angle: what automation does to Chipotle's margins" as a refused duplicate is too dismissive. It is not a new story, but it can be a valid business/investor routing of the price-freeze margin question.
"Next step: newsjack-detector" is not obviously the right first move if Chipotle owns the announcement. Proof access and journalist fit matter before hunting for an external peg.
gaps_in_B: "The prevailing belief right now is that chains pass food-cost inflation straight to the menu" is an invented consensus/current peg. Maybe true, maybe not; the supplied update does not prove it.
"Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices" overstates causality. The facts say Autocado cuts prep time and Chipotle will hold prices flat; they do not say the robot funds the freeze.
"with automation as the implied offset" decorates a hypothesis as if Chipotle implied it. A reporter can test that link, but the angle should not assert it.
"they move to the counter" narrows "redeployed to the front line" into a specific station the update never names. Small wording, real credibility leak.
